text: LEGO began in 1932 as a carpenter's workshop in Billund, Denmark, making wooden toys during the Depression. The name came from two Danish words: "leg godt." Play well.

In 1947, the carpenter, Ole Kirk Christiansen, bought a plastic injection-molding machine. It reportedly cost more than twice what the company had earned the year before. By 1949, it was making little plastic bricks.

According to LEGO's own history, in 1954 his son Godtfred heard a toy buyer complain that toys had no system. Nothing connected to anything else. So Godtfred built one. A town to build, where every piece fits every other piece, and every new set adds to the ones you already have. LEGO launched it the next year.
There was just one problem. The bricks didn't hold together very well. So Godtfred added tubes under each brick. In 1958, LEGO filed the patent. Now every brick locked.
Two years later, a fire destroyed the company's warehouse of wooden toys. LEGO didn't rebuild that part. It focused on the bricks.
Keep those two ideas in mind. A system where the same pieces keep coming back, set after set. And a company that grew stronger by doing less. Four decades later, LEGO would forget both.
